newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Dalai Lama says time's running out for Tibet pact.
newsitem.headline: Dalai Lama says time's running out for Tibet pact.

text.p: The Dalai Lama, exiled spiritual leader of Tibet, said on Thursday that time was running out to reach an agreement with China on autonomy for his homeland.
"If the present situation remains for another 10 years, then I think it may be too late," he told the National Press Club in Wellington.
"In all areas the Chinese population is greater in Tibet. Two-thirds of the population is now Chinese, only one-third Tibetan. So another 10 years, and I think really then it would be very critical."
China, which has ruled Tibet on the basis of historical claim since 1950, has refused to negotiate with the Dalai Lama, describing him as a political activist who aims to disrupt national unity.
But the Buddhist monk, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 for his peaceful campaign for self-rule in Tibet, said he believed a solution to the problem could be found.

"I have some reasons to believe that within a few years...we will find some kind of mutually agreeable solution," said the Dalai Lama who went into exile in 1959 after an abortive Tibetan uprising against Chinese rule.
"Although Chinese on (an) official level are very lacking in response towards my peaceful approach, among the Chinese people there is genuine concern and support."

The Dalai Lama is on a five-day visit to New Zealand and has met Prime Minister Jim Bolger and Foreign Minister Don McKinnon, despite Beijing's warning that such meetings would jeopardise smooth Sino-New Zealand relations.

"The Dalai Lama is not purely a religious personage but a political exile who engages in political activities aimed at disrupting national unity, advocating Tibetan independence and splitting up the motherland," a statement from the Chinese embassy in Wellington said earlier.
The Dalai Lama is touring New Zealand cities and holding public meetings on the theme "a Celebration of Kindness".
"In spite of the many drawbacks, the sympathy and support we are receiving from all over the world I think (is) very, very encouraging," the Dalai Lama said.
He said he was sure that Tibet would enjoy self-rule within his lifetime and said as soon as it was achieved, he would retire.
"Tibet's government should be democratically elected. I do not think it appropriate that a Buddhist monk work in politics."
